The UK and the European Union have struck a deal to ease
some of the trade and travel barriers that went up
when the UK left the EU in 2020.
As Villam Marx reports, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham
called it a good day for Britain.
This latest deal does away with most border checks
on British food sold into the European Union,
something UK exporters have complained about
since Brexit was finalized six years ago.
In exchange, Britain will be forced to follow
some EU rules on agricultural production.
Also, up to 100,000 young Brits will be able to live,
work, and study in the EU for up to three years,
and vice versa.
But the EU wants British universities
to charge European students less money,
and has given Britain six months to agree,
insisting the deal depends on it.
The Brexit campaigner and now leader of the UK's reform party,
Nigel Farage, says Prime Minister Burnham
has no democratic mandate to make these changes
to the existing Brexit deal.
For NPR News, I'm Villam Marx in London.
President Trump says he'll give a press conference next hour.
He's expected to discuss his trip to Asia this week.
There are questions about sales of US computer chips to China.
These are used to advance China's AI efforts,
but that could conflict with US security goals.
And Bear's Greg Myry says members of Congress
have been pushing back.
The House Foreign Affairs Committee,
headed by a Republican, Brian Mast of Florida,
took a highly unusual step yesterday.
It released a list of requests this year by Nvidia
and another chip maker, AMD,
to sell chips directly to Chinese companies.
And as of May this year, the Trump administration
had approved the sale of nearly 900,000
advanced chips to Chinese companies.
Some are very well known, like Alibaba and Tencent.
And those two companies are also on a Pentagon list
of Chinese firms linked to China's military.
And Bear's Greg Myry reporting.
The law firm Kirkland & Ellis has told Congress
it performed nearly $12 million in free legal work

This was to avoid being targeted

Democratic lawmakers are demanding answers

President Trump slapped several law firms

Several big law firms chose to settle

Kirkland & Ellis recently told House Democrats

though it balked at helping to rename the Kennedy Center
or helping Trump with some other pet projects.
Democrats wanna know if other big law firms

Kerry Johnson, NPR News.

The Iraqi government has reached a deal
with a major Iran-backed militia
over control of bases near Baghdad.
As NPR's Jane Arap reports,
the move diffuses fears over clashes
between militia fighters and Iraqi security forces.
Iraqi security officials announced Friday
that government forces would deploy to Jafar Nasser,
where Iran-backed Qatab Hezbollah has bases.
The government has accused the paramilitary group
and some government officials
of oil smuggling operations in the area south of Baghdad.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Azadi
has pledged to disarm Iraq's extensive network
of armed groups that aren't fully under government control.
While some have agreed,
Qatab Hezbollah, one of the most powerful,
has refused to give up its weapons.
Jane Arap, NPR News, Amman.
In the U.S., heavy rain this week in Florida
has triggered heavy flooding.
Some areas around Fort Lauderdale
got nearly 17 inches of rain in about 48 hours this week.
Meanwhile, the National Hurricane Center says
there is a storm system gathering
just off of Florida's Atlantic coast.
It is possible it could become a tropical storm
as it moves north along the U.S. coast.
Today is the last official day
for the United Nations Climate Summit in Turkey.
Negotiators are trying to get countries to agree
that they will cut fossil fuel emissions
and reduce global warming.
No strong agreement has yet emerged from the summit.
I'm Corva Coleman, NPR News, in Washington.
